BARCELONA, Spain — At AutoSens and InCabin Europe 2026 in Barcelona, more than 1,000 engineers, executives, and semiconductor experts gathered to examine how evolving safety, perception, and computing requirements are influencing automotive sensor design.

OEMs and Tier-1 suppliers are working together, connecting chipmakers with automotive architects. Driving this development is a wave of regulations, especially Europe’s Euro NCAP 2026 protocols, which require carmakers to go beyond conventional parts.

Euro NCAP 2026 and in-cabin safety requirements

Euro NCAP’s 2026 safety protocols put greater emphasis on driver and occupant monitoring. Driver state monitoring (DSM) is a key part of the safe driving assessment. The protocols also assess child presence detection and award additional points for systems that can detect impairment and respond when a driver becomes unresponsive.

Camera-based systems can struggle when occupants or objects are obscured, such as a baby under a blanket or sleeping in a footwell. To address these limitations without raising costs, some suppliers are combining cameras with RF sensing technologies such as UWB and mmWave radar.

At AutoSens Europe 2026, Calterah demonstrated its Dubhe CAL1106AQ SoC, which the company stated is the first implementation of IEEE 802.15.4ab sensing in a FiRa 4.0-certified 2T4R UWB chip. With its Radar Leakage Suppression module, Calterah said the chip can detect tiny movements, such as the chest of a breathing infant, without a separate mmWave radar unit.

Calterah stated that its Bluetooth Low Energy-assisted multi-millisecond system can measure distances over 400 meters, even through parked cars. The company said the UWB upgrade can support child presence detection by updating existing keyless entry hardware with new software, which could make dedicated 60 GHz mmWave interior radars less necessary.

Meanwhile, Infineon Technologies showcased its XENSIV 60 GHz radar evaluation modules, demonstrating full-cabin monitoring and real-time radar point cloud overlays on live video feeds.

Advanced optical vision

Even with new RF technologies that can sense movement through obstacles, optical cameras are still essential for capturing detailed information inside the car.

Optical cameras can identify who is in the car, check where people are looking to see if they are distracted, and read small facial expressions to spot fatigue.

At the show, Omnivision demonstrated its OX05C1S GS HDR sensor, which uses Nyxel near-infrared technology to achieve high-resolution imaging in near-dark conditions. By shrinking its package by 30%, OmniVision said it allows unobtrusive integration into rearview mirrors or vehicle pillars.

In parallel, Tier-1 supplier Aptiv showcased its Advanced Occupancy Classification software, using a single interior camera to differentiate between adults, infants, children, and inanimate objects.

Aptiv said this camera-only method reached 100% accuracy in Federal Motor Vehicle Safety Standard 208 tests, a U.S. regulation, and cut system costs by up to 40% by removing the need for in-seat pressure sensors.

Exterior perception by single-exposure HDR and imaging radar

For outside driver assistance and self-driving features, engineers have to deal with problems such as bright sun glare, dark tunnels, and flickering LED traffic lights.

To address these challenges, Omnivision presented its 3MP TheiaCel image sensor, which offers 140 decibels of single-exposure high dynamic range. Unlike older multi-exposure methods that can cause motion blur at high speeds, the company said this single-exposure approach keeps images clear in bright and dark areas and reduces flicker.

Similarly, SmartSens Technology showed its 8.3MP SC860AT CMOS sensor, which features Lofic HDR 2.0 and is compliant with ISO 26262 ASIL-B and ISO 21434. The sensor was demonstrated with SmartSens subsidiary Flyingchip’s M2 automotive vision-processing SoC, which integrates a neural processing unit and complies with AEC-Q100 Grade 2 automotive standards and ISO 26262 ASIL-B/D functional safety levels.

On the central computing side, Samsung showed its ISOCELL Auto 1H1 and 4AC image sensors alongside a virtual validation partnership with Synopsys and Ansys. Incorporating digital twin models of Samsung sensors into simulation software enables virtual perception validation, shortening product development cycles by up to 12 months, the company said.

Different compute architectures

Discussions about vehicle computing indicated a move away from full centralization toward smarter zonal processing. Automakers used to want all processing in one central computer, but, at AutoSens USA 2026, experts from NXP, Stellantis, and Bosch, pointed out that this causes heat problems and needs too much wiring. Now, the industry is moving to zonal systems, where AI processing happens at the edge, and only key data goes back to the main processor.

Demonstrating this edge-compute trend, STMicroelectronics showcased its STM32N6 microcontroller, featuring an integrated Neural-ART NPU delivering 600 billion operations per second at 3 TOPS per watt. The company showed a demo that included real-time face recognition running directly on the microcontroller.

Meanwhile, high-speed data transfer sparked competition between networking standards. Valens Semiconductor showed its VA7000 chipsets supporting MIPI A-PHY, while Omnivision showcased its 3MP camera sensor featuring an integrated Automotive SerDes Alliance Motion Link serializer.

Cybersecurity and post-quantum cryptography

As software-defined vehicles become increasingly connected, regulatory oversight is expanding beyond standard automotive rules to encompass the European Cyber Resilience Act.

The regulation mandates strict cybersecurity baselines, vulnerability patching, and hardware secure-boot mechanisms for digital products in Europe. Separately, the U.S. National Security Agency’s CNSA 2.0 requirements mandate a transition to post-quantum cryptography to defend against future quantum computing attacks.

At AutoSens Europe, Microchip showed its Trust Shield TS1800 and TS50x Platform root of trust controllers, using an Arm Cortex-M4F processor to run lattice-based post-quantum cryptographic algorithms. The hardware anchors trust directly in physical silicon by monitoring flash memory in real time to prevent firmware tampering.

data.title: Continuous Health Monitoring Drives Integrated Wearable System Design
data.description:
//php echo do_shortcode('[responsivevoice_button voice="US English Male" buttontext="Listen to Post"]') ?>

The smaller a wearable electronics gadget gets, the more it has to do. A device that once tracked steps and heart rate now has to continuously capture physiological signals while making room for more sensors, optics, processing, and power management. That is pushing wearable designers to treat the optical, mechanical, sensing, and power domains as a connected system, rather than designing each function separately.

“We are seeing a lot of integration happening in devices,” said Praveen Jose, senior technical leader, field applications, at Analog Devices India, during a press briefing organized by the company. “Your devices become smaller and smaller, but the quality of the devices or the quality of the performance is increasing.”

Jose said the challenge is how to accommodate more functions within a small device and make it a single-body solution.

Sensio, an Indian startup developing smart rings, smart bands, and patches, focuses on wellness and health and claims its wearables collect heart rate, respiratory rate, blood oxygen, temperature, sleep, and activity data.

At the press briefing, Venkatesh Vadde, co-founder and CEO of Sensio, described how electrocardiogram (ECG) and photoplethysmography (PPG) can be used to estimate blood pressure continuously without a cuff, although he noted that the approach does not provide absolute blood pressure.

He said the startup works on embedding sensors in wearable devices, placing them at the right point, optimizing the signal, and using algorithms to interpret raw physiological signals.

That puts the optical path, sensor position, and physical construction of the wearable closer to the semiconductor design problem. Vadde said Sensio works with ADI sensors and other components and optimizes sensor placement, housing, and optics as part of the wearable design.

Identifying the problems

Jose said that optical sensing is challenging because the required physiological signal is embedded in noise. The sensing system needs to capture the required signal in the presence of noise before the data can be processed by algorithms or AI.

“In that particular scenario, you need to have a very good device which can actually sense the data in the presence of noise,” he said. “How accurately you can sense it is what will give you better data.”

For a wearable designer, that means the optical assembly, sensor position, and mechanical construction can affect the quality of the electrical signal coming from the sensor. Vadde highlighted how closely the mechanical and optical aspects of the wearable are linked to PPG performance. The placement of the optical assembly relative to the skin affects the signal.

“Even a fraction of a millimeter lift-off of the optical assembly from the skin impacts PPG,” Vadde said.

The enclosure, housing, skin contact, optical assembly, and sensor placement therefore all have a bearing on the signal ultimately processed by the device.

For a ring, this becomes particularly important because the device has to maintain consistent contact with the skin while remaining small enough to be worn continuously, including during sleep.

The same system-level problem appears when the wearer moves. Vadde said motion artefacts, power consumption, and signal quality are real design challenges in wearable devices. The optics, mechanics, and housing have to be considered together.

This brings an accelerometer or inertial measurement unit (IMU) into the physiological sensing chain. In a consumer wearable, an accelerometer can be used to determine activity or movement. In a health-monitoring wearable, motion information can also help identify periods when another physiological measurement may be affected by motion artefacts.

Vadde said an IMU can be used to screen motion artefacts so that the system accepts higher-quality physiological data.

Jose described motion and activity detection as one of the functions being integrated into wearable platforms. “When we have something that we want to monitor, what we want to have is the motion to be sensed,” he said.

The signal quality can also affect power consumption. Vadde pointed to automatic gain control (AGC) as an example. When optical coupling or motion affects the quality of the signal, the system can increase the gain to recover the required signal. Depending on the implementation, that can also affect power consumption.

This creates a chain of interdependent design decisions—optical and mechanical design affect signal quality; signal quality affects analog processing and gain; processing affects power consumption; and power consumption affects battery life.

The power architecture also has to account for sensing frequency, processing, connectivity, and periods when the device does not need to operate at full activity. “Sometimes what happens is, when a person is taking rest, and we know that during different conditions more power is needed by the product, we will go into sleep mode or deep sleep mode, and the effect is to retain the battery power,” Jose said.

Connectivity is another consideration. Jose described the requirement as low-power to medium-power connectivity for continuous monitoring applications.

The frequency at which measurements are taken also affects battery life. Vadde said the required frequency of vital-sign measurements depends on the patient and the context. Taking measurements less frequently can extend battery life, while storing and synchronizing data rather than continuously transmitting it can also affect power consumption.

Combining sensing and power functions

The system-level problem is also shaping the way ADI approaches wearable customers. Vivek Tyagi, managing director, sales and country leader, at Analog Devices India, said the company sees two distinct types of customers: those with the capability to integrate optical components and those that require an easier-to-integrate approach.

Tyagi said the company has developed two types of solutions: sensor-hub devices that are easier for customers to use, and standalone solutions that he said can provide higher accuracy but require customers to have greater precision in integrating the optics, LEDs, and other elements.

ADI is also working on integrating sensing, power management, charging, and battery management functions. The company is also working on low-power solutions for applications such as continuous glucose monitoring. With ADI’s work on energy harvesting, mechanical movement or a temperature gradient can be converted into a small amount of electrical power that can be used to charge the device and extend battery life.

Jose said ADI’s solutions cover PPG, temperature sensing, ECG, and accelerometers, alongside power and connectivity functions.

For ring applications, Jose referred to Analog Devices MAX86178, while Vikash Singh, product application staff engineer, Healthcare Marketing and Applications, at Analog Devices India, described the MAX86184 as a small-form-factor PPG analog front end (AFE) designed for ring applications, with support for up to 14 LEDs and four photodiodes and dual-channel capability.

The MAX86178 is a more broadly integrated vital-sign analog front end (AFE) that combines PPG, ECG, and BioZ functions; its PPG section supports up to six LEDs and four photodiode inputs.

ADI is trying to bring more of the functions required by the wearable into fewer devices, while leaving customers with different levels of integration depending on their optical and system-design capabilities.

Tyagi said ADI is engaging customers earlier in their product roadmaps to understand what they want to build two or three years ahead and then co-create solutions.

“Then engage with a strategic partnership early on in their design journey, so that we can co-create a solution,” he said.

The sensing chain becomes the design problem

The trend toward continuous health monitoring is changing what has to be considered when designing a wearable.

Temperature sensors have to fit within small form factors while maintaining accuracy. Optical sensors have to extract physiological signals from noisy environments. Mechanical construction and sensor placement affect optical coupling. Motion information can be used to identify artefacts. Analog processing can compensate for weak signals but may affect power consumption. Connectivity has to transmit or synchronize the resulting data without exhausting the battery.

Jose said the quality of the sensed data is central to continuous monitoring. “How accurately you can sense it is what will give you better data,” he said.

For wearable designers, the implication is that the sensing problem extends beyond an individual sensor. Optical and mechanical design, motion sensing, analog processing, algorithms, connectivity, and power all affect how a wearable collects and handles physiological data over time.

As wearables move from tracking activity toward continuous health monitoring, the engineering challenge is increasingly how these functions work together inside a device with very little room for error and physical space.

Tirias Research principal analysts Jim McGregor and Francis Sideco were on the ground in Maui, Hawaii, for Qualcomm’s annual Snapdragon Summit. This year’s event was all about personal agentic AI, with updates to Qualcomm’s Mobile, Hearables/Wearables, and PC solutions. Specifically, for smartphones, Qualcomm announced not one but two next-generation additions to its flagship Snapdragon 8 Elite portfolio: the Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 6 and Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6.

While others might have simply derived two SKUs from the same basic chip design, Qualcomm literally doubled down on high-end smartphones with two distinct SoCs—essentially compressing six years of development into three. This begs two loaded questions: How? And why? 

In this video, McGregor and Sideco answer these questions along with updates to Qualcomm’s Wearables/Hearables, and PC solutions and how they will impact personalized agentic AI over the next one to three years.

data.description:

BUDAPEST, Hungary — At the Pretzel Connect 2026 press event, Kate Underhill, future space transportation propulsion architect at the European Space Agency (ESA), emphasized that future launch systems and orbital infrastructure will depend as much on onboard computing, automation, and strong connectivity, as on advances in propulsion.

These dependencies expose the European space sector to wider geopolitical risks, especially in semiconductor manufacturing, raw material supply chains, and international regulations.

Silicon bottleneck

In a conversation with EE Times, Underhill expressed concerns about Europe’s reliance on foreign semiconductors and how this affects industrial strategy. As most advanced semiconductor manufacturing happens outside Europe, it creates risks for industries such as automotive, telecom, and space hardware.

Underhill detailed the historical technology gap between commercial microelectronics and flight-qualified space hardware. Space programs have traditionally relied on older, radiation-tolerant processors, such as the SPARC-based LEON family that ESA began developing in 1997, to withstand harsh orbital radiation.

“We are very conservative in space, and we have a very specific environment for electronics,” Underhill stated, observing that space systems typically operate “at least 10 years behind consumer electronics.”

This technology gap is made worse by tough buying conditions. She gave an example in which ESA tried to order just 20 laser diodes from a German company, but the supplier required a minimum order of 10,000 units.

“We have that issue,” Underhill explained, noting that low satellite launch volumes prevent space component buyers from securing favorable pricing. To address this cost penalty, ESA is pursuing “spin-in” strategies that adapt high-volume commercial off-the-shelf electronics for spaceflight, while seeking “spin-out” opportunities where space-tested designs can enter commercial terrestrial markets.

Strategic independence

The discussion shifted to technological independence and export controls, which are now urgent topics in European policy. For example, companies such as Nokia and Ericsson lead in building telecom networks, but their supply chains remain vulnerable to foreign policy changes.

Underhill explained that European satellite developers often face compliance challenges tied to U.S. export regulations, specifically the International Traffic in Arms Regulations (ITAR). “If there is any U.S. component on your satellite, then you have to comply with U.S. regulations,” Underhill said.

In her keynote, Underhill cited efforts by European manufacturers to construct ITAR-free satellites, which have faced persistent hurdles because certain specialized parts remain available only from foreign suppliers. “We need to identify the components we are still buying from the U.S. or from China and see what we can do in Europe so that we can have control over the complete supply chain as much as possible,” Underhill stated.

Outlining ESA’s role in safeguarding sovereign capabilities, she emphasized that independent access to space is fundamental to economic stability. “For minimum critical elements, we need access to space,” Underhill said. “We need positioning, telecoms, and earth observation data. We need that in Europe and full control over that.”

Next-generation satellite networks and 6G

Combining satellite networks with new cellular standards is a major growth area for European telecom companies. International groups are working to include satellite networks in 6G standards, which could allow direct connections to phones without special ground equipment.

Underhill pointed to Europe’s planned IRIS² secure satellite constellation as a project that will transform European space manufacturing through scale. Under an implementation agreement signed by the European Commission and the SpaceRISE consortium on Aug. 7, 2026, the constellation will comprise 348 satellites, shifting the sector away from custom, single-unit fabrication. Underhill said the program moves the sector from building “this one satellite” to making hundreds, at which point “the order quantities move into semi-industrialized levels, and we can start taking advantage of that scale.”

On integrating 6G and satellite connectivity, Underhill noted that building the infrastructure will unlock commercial use cases developers cannot fully predict. Comparing the trend to Earth observation data, which began for climate monitoring but is now used for agriculture and municipal tax assessment, she argued that ubiquitous orbital data pipes will drive widespread innovation.

“This is critical infrastructure for Europe,” Underhill emphasized. “If we have 6G, if we have IRIS² operational, if we have Galileo plus 6G… there are lots of clever people in young companies in Europe that can do some really good stuff with that.” She added succinctly: “Once the system is there, people use it.”

Industrial scale and cost

Beyond telecommunications, Underhill addressed economic pressures reshaping launch operations globally. Europe’s Ariane 5, retired in July 2023, flew six to seven missions a year at its peak, with costs of around $10,000 per kg of payload.

By comparison, Underhill said SpaceX is targeting launch costs as low as $30 per kilogram with a fully reusable Starship. That remains an aspiration: In a July 30 post on X, SpaceX CEO Elon Musk has recently said costs could fall below $100 per kilogram, but only if full reusability and local propellant production are achieved. A 2026 White House memo sets a target for U.S. infrastructure to support more than 1,000 launches and reentries annually by 2030. Arianespace has set a target cadence of nine to 10 Ariane 6 launches a year from 2027, while Avio, which builds and markets the smaller Vega-C, is working toward six launches a year.

Underhill said that Europe needs to make its space transportation similar to the airline industry, with quick turnarounds, predictive maintenance, and frequent launches. “The traditional way we build launchers cannot provide that, so we have to rethink it,” she said.

To reach these goals, Underhill highlighted, ESA is using AI in design, testing, and manufacturing. AI lets engineers run complex simulations, reducing the need for physical testing. Digital twins of rocket engines help monitor their health and predict how long they will last. In 3D printing, AI checks each layer during production to ensure parts are strong and defect-free.

Environmental and regulatory challenges

Her keynote also covered the rules for making space hardware, especially environmental standards and limits on certain chemicals.

Underhill expressed concerns about a proposed EU restriction on PFAS, a group of synthetic chemicals that persist in the environment. She said that while ESA supports protecting the environment, some of these chemicals are still needed for extreme aerospace conditions.

“I cannot make a cryogenic system without PFAS in my seals,” Underhill said, explaining that ESA is working directly with European regulators to secure temporary exemptions while simultaneously funding research into eco-friendly alternatives. “We are launching projects with European companies to get PFAS-free seals, and it will take us five, six, seven years to get something,” she stated.

Underhill finished by comparing Europe’s regulatory approach with other spacefaring countries. She said that while places such as the U.S. have fewer rules and can move faster in the short term, Europe’s strict standards for the environment, labor, and safety help build long-term strength in the industry.

“The regulatory environment in Europe is different, and we do have more regulations than in the U.S., which can be complicated and can slow things down, but do enable long-term human things that work on the longer term,” Underhill concluded.

Through programs such as FLPP and the FIRST initiative, ESA is working with European industry to prepare for new regulations and reduce the risk of future supply-chain disruptions.

data.title: Emergence AI to Deploy Neuroformal AI With Fabless Chipmakers
data.description:
//php echo do_shortcode('[responsivevoice_button voice="US English Male" buttontext="Listen to Post"]') ?>

Emergence AI said it is moving its neuroformal AI technology into active deployments with fabless semiconductor companies, while integrated device manufacturers (IDMs) among its customers are asking the company to extend the work into the fab.

The startup also targets the data generated during manufacturing to identify early signs of degradation before a problem affects a large number of wafers.

In an interview with EE Times at SEMICON India 2026, Satya Nitta, co-founder and executive chairman of Emergence AI, said, “You cannot make chips any faster, but what you can do is definitely get more chips per wafer yielding with AI.”

Nitta said demand for chips exceeds supply and every fab is running at capacity, so more wafers cannot be pushed through. The way to ease the shortage is to get more chips per wafer yielding, which requires analyzing the data, he said.

Nitta said neuroformal AI pairs the creativity of large language models (LLMs) with the discipline of symbolic AI, an older approach based on formal rules that was “all of AI” before the deep learning era. “Algorithms propose, and symbolic AI verifies,” he said. The aim is to develop AI that gives “provably correct” answers that engineers can depend on for mission-critical problems, because LLMs are probabilistic.

Nitta became executive chairman and chief scientist about a month ago, when Emergence AI appointed Ian Eslick as CEO, according to a LinkedIn post by Nitta. He said he will lead the company’s long-term research agenda, advance neuroformal AI, and deepen key partnerships, while Eslick leads the company through its next stage of commercialization and scale.

Eslick founded Silicon Spice, an MIT spinout that Broadcom acquired for $1.2 billion, and later led major technology initiatives at U.S. Bank and SoFi, according to the post.

Fabless companies and yield analysis

Nitta said Emergence AI started with the fabless part of the semiconductor value chain. Fabless companies design the product but do not control the manufacturing process, he said. They have data on the chip itself, such as functional, parametric, and overall yield, but not on what happens in the fab.

He said the analysis can show whether a yield excursion stems from a process issue in the fab, a design issue, or a test issue. “Wafer and final test issues are not uncommon,” he said. “The probe cards do not make perfect contact. I may have to retest it.”

He said AI agents can analyze this data at scale and remember patterns seen across products. As an example, he described an agent that finds the same pattern across 30% of 1,500 products, with failures in a ring oscillator block, and suggests redesigning that block. “These are the kinds of things that AI agents can do that are beyond human cognitive limits,” he said.

Nitta said the company’s domain-specific agents also carry out root-cause analysis. They have to distinguish a spurious correlation from the actual cause, using an understanding of device physics.

Asked whether the company competes with today’s LLMs and GPTs, Nitta said, “I would not say directly competing. We are saying that the LLMs are necessary but not sufficient.” He also said LLM-based AI is “useful but incomplete for mission-critical problems.”

Physics-driven failures in advanced packaging

Nitta said the company is beginning to move into advanced packaging. Because many packaging technologies are still being developed, he said, the question is less about what went wrong in the process and more about fundamental root causes.

One example is a coefficient of thermal expansion (CTE) mismatch. “It is much more a physics problem,” he said.

He said AI agents would need to run finite-element and multiscale physics simulations to show, for example, that a liner material and copper are incompatible, or that a glass substrate and copper have a large CTE mismatch, causing things to fall apart in thermal cycling. He said that if the via were redesigned, the aspect ratio changed, or the liner thickness increased, “the process window is more mature.”

Nitta said Emergence AI is in active discussions with several advanced packaging companies that could lead to memoranda of understanding. He said he expects several announcements about these engagements in the next two to three months. The company has no active engagements with semiconductor tooling companies, he said.

Nitta said some of the fabless customers are IDMs, which have “both the fabless component and fabs.” The work starts in the fabless part, he said, and the IDMs are now asking the company to work in the fab. The work in the fab is “still at a very early stage,” he added.

Some of the fabless customers are among the largest companies in the industry but he could not name them on the record.

India: focus, talent, and open-source

In India, the company’s focus is limited to semiconductors, Nitta said. Emergence AI is primarily working post-tape-out and is not currently involved in chip design, though that could change in the future. He said verification is one of the longest steps in chip design and that neuroformal AI can accelerate the process.

The company is also talking with several potential Indian customers, but Nitta said he could not name them. “We are in the middle of several discussions,” he said.

Nitta said Emergence AI intends to grow its talent pool to 500 engineers and R&D scientists within two years. EE Times had earlier reported a timeframe of three to four years.

This summer, the company conducted a summer school on Lean, an open-source programming language and proof assistant, for more than 150 students, under the guidance of professor Siddharth Gadgil, chief scientist of Emergence India Labs and a professor at the Indian Institute of Science (IISc), and professor Ilya Sergey at the National University of Singapore. Nitta said talent for this work is scarce, so the company is creating it. The company has identified a group of people to whom it is extending talent retention offers.

Nitta said the company has open-sourced parts of its technology from the beginning and is now open-sourcing some of its Lean work with Gadgil and Emergence India Labs. He said aspects of the neuroformal AI work will also be open-sourced to build a community and widen the pool from which the company recruits.

He pointed to Agent-E, an open-source web navigation system the company released in 2024 that automates complex browser tasks using simple natural language. He described it as “the very first autonomous web agent build that was fully open-source” and “the very first time somebody actually open-sourced a complex hierarchical agentic system.” Agent-E is available on GitHub. Nitta indicated that the neuroformal AI work will follow a similar path.

He added that the semiconductor industry is only beginning to explore what autonomous agents can do. “I am delighted to see that even in India, there is enormous growth and support from the central government,” Nitta said. “But we are just scratching the surface.”

data.title: AI Drives Larger, Denser Packaging, Raising New Challenges for Equipment Makers
data.description:
//php echo do_shortcode('[responsivevoice_button voice="US English Male" buttontext="Listen to Post"]') ?>

Artificial intelligence is pushing advanced packaging in seemingly opposite directions: Package sizes are getting larger, while interconnect pitches and defect tolerances continue to shrink.

At A*STAR’s Innovate Together 2026 in Singapore, experts from KLA, ASM, ASMPT, and the National University of Singapore (NUS) discussed how advanced packaging is evolving beyond individual equipment or process technologies. The challenge is to integrate materials, bonding, metrology and inspection, optical interconnects, and system design while maintaining yield, reliability, and cost efficiency across larger package areas and finer interconnect pitches.

Surya Bhattacharya, head of system-in-package at A*STAR’s Institute of Microelectronics (IME) and moderator of the panel, said that as continued transistor scaling becomes insufficient to meet AI computing demands, systems must integrate more dies and functions, making packaging an increasingly integral part of system design.

Hybrid bonding puts materials and processes to the test

Avi Shantaram, corporate director of advanced packaging at ASM International, said hybrid bonding is an important technology for next-generation, high-density 3D interconnects, but the challenge extends well beyond the bonding equipment itself. Interface engineering is equally critical.

As chiplets and 3D stacking drive higher interconnect densities, wafer surface roughness, chemical mechanical polishing (CMP) dishing, cleanliness, and particle control can all affect bonding results. Hybrid bonding requires highly flat and clean surfaces, making precursor characteristics, CMP, atomic layer deposition, surface treatment, materials interface engineering, and low-temperature processing important elements of process control.

As interconnect dimensions shrink, even tiny particles can create much larger voids at the bonding interface, potentially affecting reliability and yield.

Gary Widdowson, senior VP and CTO of ASMPT’s semiconductor solutions, said hybrid bonding will not immediately replace conventional thermal compression bonding (TCB). TCB still offers advantages in process maturity and cost, and the two technologies are likely to coexist at different stages, particularly in high-density stacking applications such as high-bandwidth memory (HBM).

However, as interconnect pitch continues to shrink, the advantages of direct copper-to-copper bonding for high-density interconnects could make hybrid bonding necessary for some advanced packages.

The pace of adoption will ultimately depend on both cost and yield, Widdowson said. “We are dealing with a complete process, not a single equipment problem.” Equipment makers therefore need to work with wafer manufacturers, packaging companies, and materials suppliers to establish process windows that can take hybrid bonding from technology demonstrations into high-volume manufacturing (HVM).

HBM raises the bar for advanced packaging process control

When HBM and multiple logic dies are integrated into a single package, small process variations can become system-level yield problems. Chia Wee Teck, VP and general manager of KLA’s Global Customer Organization, said advanced packaging cannot rely solely on final inspection; defects and process variation must be monitored throughout the manufacturing flow.

“If you can’t see it, you can’t measure it, you can’t control it,” Chia said. Equipment makers need to connect inspection, metrology, and process data to identify the sources of defects and feed the information back into the process, creating a continuous control loop.

For HBM and hybrid bonding, this means monitoring high-density interconnects, fine pitches, copper surface profiles, bond voids, surface contamination, and die and wafer geometry. As packages move from engineering validation into HVM, turning these data into controllable process windows will be critical to yield and reliability.

KLA’s collaboration with A*STAR focuses on advanced packaging process control, using inspection and metrology to identify defects earlier and monitor process variation.

Optical interconnects emerge as another AI packaging bottleneck

Data movement is emerging as another bottleneck for AI systems. Aaron Thean, deputy president (Academic Affairs) and provost of NUS and director of SHINE, said the importance of optical interconnects is increasing as AI computing scales, with data rates moving from 200 Gb/s per lane toward 400 Gb/s per lane and beyond.

This means photonics can no longer be treated simply as a collection of discrete components. It must be designed together with electronics, packaging, and the overall system architecture. Future heterogeneous integration will need to incorporate photonic components at the system level, including light-source integration and connections between optoelectronic components.

Thean also pointed to materials such as lithium niobate as potential options for high-speed photonic devices.

From an equipment and packaging perspective, Widdowson noted that optical interconnects bring together a range of components, including electronic integrated circuits (EICs), photonic integrated circuits (PICs), laser diodes, fiber arrays, and microlenses. While each component may be relatively mature on its own, integrating them into a single package introduces challenges in alignment, bonding, thermal management, and reliability.

Chia said the greater challenge is integrating multiple optical and electronic components while maintaining yield, reliability, and cost efficiency. As co-packaged optics (CPO) and near-package optics (NPO) move toward tighter integration with compute and switch chips, packaging process control will become increasingly important.

Panel-level packaging amplifies manufacturing challenges

As AI systems integrate more dies into a single package, package size is also becoming a manufacturing-efficiency issue. Bhattacharya said that as high-performance computing systems scale, packages may need to accommodate larger compute and memory components. Even when package sizes reach 9× the reticle or beyond, manufacturing packages or interposers on a 300-mm wafer becomes increasingly inefficient, prompting the industry to consider larger panel-based platforms.

Widdowson said the industry is exploring a range of panel sizes, starting at roughly the 300-mm class and extending to 600 mm, 700 mm, 800 mm, and even close to 1 m. There is no industry consensus yet on a final panel size, although 510 × 515 mm is among the dimensions currently being discussed. Standards will be needed for panel dimensions, equipment interfaces, and infrastructure to avoid unnecessary complexity across the manufacturing ecosystem.

Larger panels, however, introduce new process control challenges. Chia noted that large, heavy panels can suffer from warpage and distortion and create handling difficulties. Maintaining inspection capability for fine-pitch routing across a much larger area is also challenging.

At the same time, package areas are expanding while defect sizes are not—and may continue to shrink. Equipment makers therefore need to maintain nanometer-level inspection and metrology across increasingly large manufacturing areas, while feeding the results back into materials, bonding, CMP, and other processes. The goal is to enable advanced packaging to continue scaling toward both higher density and larger package sizes.

The memory wall is seen as the biggest hurdle for rapidly scaling AI deployments, and moving memory closer to compute is seen as the optimal solution to the problem.

Astera Labs’ update to its Leo Smart Memory Controller family aims to do exactly that. The company’s new Leo X-Series fabric-attached memory controller, along with the next-generation Leo 2 E-Series and P-Series controllers, is designed to optimize memory performance as LLMs evolve into multi-turn agentic systems.

In a briefing with EE Times, Thad Omura, senior VP of Astera Labs’ compute connectivity group, said memory is the central infrastructure challenge as it races to keep up with the advances in GPU clustering during the early AI boom. “All the bottlenecks around memory are back and driving new architectures, and we’re trying to deal with the memory constraints,” he said.

The Leo 2 E-Series and P-Series continue Astera Labs’ CXL-based strategy for CPU-attached memory expansion and pooling. The devices support both DDR5 and reused DDR4 memory, offering up to 4 TB of DDR5 capacity per controller and up to 768 GB of repurposed DDR4. The company has also added memory testing, telemetry, predictive failure analysis, and automated repair capabilities to help hyperscalers redeploy aging DIMMs.

In benchmark testing using four Nvidia H200 GPUs running the Qwen2.5-32B model with multi-turn agentic workloads, Astera Labs reported a 62% reduction in time-to-first-token (TTFT) and a 22% increase in tokens per second compared with conventional CPU-DRAM-based KV cache offloading.

The memory wall is not the only pressure faced by AI adopters. In the same briefing, Ahmad Danesh, associate VP of product management, said DDR5 pricing has risen sharply as memory manufacturers prioritize high-bandwidth memory production. “There’s this big supply crunch and wafer supply crunch because of AI.”

Dynamic pooling and sharing features in the Leo 2 family are designed to reduce stranded memory and allow capacity to be allocated across servers as needed. “The expanded Leo family turns idle, stranded capacity into memory an AI agent can actually use, on hardware operators already own,” Omura said. “That stranded DRAM is the industry’s next scale-up resource.”

The Leo X-Series was developed specifically for inference workloads in which key-value (KV) cache data can overwhelm GPU high-bandwidth memory. Rather than routing data through CPU memory, the controller works in conjunction with Astera Labs’ Scorpio fabric switches to create a dedicated memory tier attached directly to the PCIe fabric.

Scorpio’s role is to optimize connectivity to AI accelerators and improve performance per watt, an increasingly important metric for data center operators. Astera Labs announced its latest Scorpio fabric switch earlier this year. In a briefing, Omura said fabric is the difference between peak and wasted compute.

He said the Scorpio X-Series 320-Lane Smart Fabric Switch reflects the company’s core mission of delivering purpose-built connectivity for rack-scale AI.

“Everything is measured in gigawatts,” Omura added, with scalability and resilience being equally important metrics, especially as inference grows at unprecedented scale.

Danesh said the latest Scorpio switch was built with large AI clusters in mind. It reduces latency by having a single hop for GPU communication.

To deliver that improved performance with lower power, Astera Labs has integrated dedicated hardware acceleration engines inside the chip, Danesh said. “Those engines are built to maximize the token economics further and get better performance per watt.”

He said Astera Labs’ hardware-accelerated and in-network compute engines can boost collective operations by up to 2×. For example, the in-network compute engine offloads some calculations off the accelerator. “We can calculate inside of our silicon,” Danesh said. “You’re spending less time sending the data and more time on the compute, which ultimately increases the GPU utilization.”

In addition to dedicated hardware inside Astera Labs’ silicon, the company’s Cosmos software adds another layer of intelligence. “The scale at which things are being deployed, it’s that software that really provides a lot of value,” Danesh said.

Danesh said the combination of hardware and software reflects a broader shift in AI infrastructure design; interconnects are no longer passive plumbing, but active system components that shape GPU utilization, quality of service, resilience, and the economic return on data center power budgets.

CXL has become an essential tool unlocking memory capacity to meet AI workload demands. Astera Labs released its Leo CXL Memory Accelerator Platform five years ago to enable CPUs to access and manage CXL-attached DRAM and persistent memory, making the use of centralized memory resources more efficient and allowing that access to scale up without slowing down performance.

South Korean startup Xcena also sees optimizing data movement as a critical path to address memory bottlenecks with its recently unveiled CXL Type 3 device that combines up to 2 TB of DDR5, SSD-backed InfiniteMemory capacity, and more than 1,000 custom RISC-V cores to push compute into memory.

Synopsys’s latest CXL offerings also address constrained memory capacity and bandwidth, while aiming to make the protocol easier to adopt. Marvell, meanwhile, released a suite of memory infrastructure products that aim to help hyperscale and cloud customers move memory closer to the point of computation, reduce data bottlenecks, and improve token efficiency for inference workloads.

data.title: AI Data Centers Make Power, Cooling Critical to Scaling
data.description:
//php echo do_shortcode('[responsivevoice_button voice="US English Male" buttontext="Listen to Post"]') ?>

AI is reshaping the role of data centers, turning them from largely invisible cloud infrastructure into strategic assets where power delivery, cooling, advanced packaging, and semiconductors have become as critical as compute performance.

Speaking at EE Power Asia 2026, Ang Wee Seng, executive director of the Singapore Semiconductor Industry Association (SSIA), said AI has shifted the industry’s focus beyond processor performance toward the physical infrastructure required to deploy and scale AI systems.

“AI has transformed computing from a digital challenge into a physical infrastructure race,” he said. “AI is not only about software revolution anymore. It is an infrastructure revolution.”

According to Ang, traditional measures of computing progress such as processor speed and transistor density remain important, but AI deployment increasingly depends on factors including available power, rack density, cooling capacity, memory bandwidth, and deployment speed. Large AI data centers can already draw more than 100 MW of power, while worldwide data center spending is expected to exceed $650 billion this year.

The rapid expansion of AI infrastructure is being driven by four major trends: the transition from model training to continuous inference, growing memory and bandwidth requirements, increasing investment in sovereign AI infrastructure, and ongoing cloud modernization centered on accelerated computing.

These shifts are creating new engineering constraints. “The next bottleneck may not be, can we design the next chip? It may be, can we power it? Can we connect it? Can we cool it down? Can we deploy it fast enough?” Ang said.

Infrastructure becomes the limiting factor

Ang noted that site selection for hyperscale AI facilities is increasingly determined by access to power rather than land availability. Grid connectivity, substations, cooling infrastructure, renewable energy availability, and fiber connectivity have become key considerations.

“In many cases, facility follows where the power is, not the other way around,” he said.

Energy efficiency has also become a central design objective. Every watt consumed ultimately generates heat, increasing cooling requirements and adding further power demand. Improvements in power conversion efficiency therefore translate directly into greater usable compute capacity.

“The power chain is no longer peripheral” Ang said. “It is part of the AI scaling roadmap now.”

At the system level, AI is also changing data center architecture. Rather than treating servers as independent units, AI deployments increasingly organize accelerators, networking, power delivery, and cooling around tightly integrated rack-scale systems.

“The rack is becoming the new unit of design,” Ang said. “The system is the product. The rack is the platform. The power architecture is the competitive differentiator.”

Semiconductor ecosystem expands beyond processors

While GPUs have become the focal point of AI computing, Ang said future AI platforms will rely on heterogeneous computing architectures combining CPUs, GPUs, DPUs, custom accelerators and high-speed interconnects.

Advanced packaging, chiplets, high-bandwidth memory (HBM), silicon photonics, and optical networking have consequently become integral to AI system design.

“Memory bandwidth is now central to AI scaling,” he said, noting that HBM shortages and advanced packaging capacity have become strategic constraints across the semiconductor supply chain.

He added that optimizing AI infrastructure now requires balancing silicon, packaging, boards, cooling systems, networking, and power delivery rather than maximizing the performance of individual components.

Power electronics move to center stage

Ang argued that power semiconductors are moving from supporting technologies to strategic enablers of AI infrastructure.

Power enters AI facilities through multiple conversion stages—from utility grids and UPS systems to rack-level power shelves and voltage regulators—where even small efficiency gains can significantly reduce heat generation and operating costs at hyperscale.

He highlighted complementary roles for silicon, silicon carbide (SiC) and gallium nitride (GaN), emphasizing that each technology addresses different parts of the power architecture.

“The question is not simply which material should win,” Ang said. “The better question to ask is, where does each technology create the greatest system level value?”

Looking ahead, Ang said future AI infrastructure should be evaluated using broader system metrics such as tokens per joule, watts per square meter, conversion efficiency, and deployment speed rather than compute performance alone.

“The future data centers will not be won by the fastest chip alone,” he said. “It will be won by the most efficient integrated system.”

He concluded that the semiconductor industry’s next opportunity extends across the full AI infrastructure stack, from power devices and packaging to materials, testing, and system integration.

“For years now, the semiconductor industry has powered the digital economy,” Ang said. “Now we are being asked to power the AI economy.”

 —This article was originally published in the EE Times Recommend ASEAN e-guide July 2026.

//php echo do_shortcode('[responsivevoice_button voice="US English Male" buttontext="Listen to Post"]') ?>

A free online quantum computing course co-created by IBM and IIT Madras recorded 208,785 enrollments in India in 2026, including more than 100,000 from Andhra Pradesh, according to IBM.

At SEMICON India 2026, EE Times spoke to Rahul Rao, distinguished engineer in processor design at IBM’s India Systems Development Lab (ISDL), about IBM’s integration of Qiskit into India’s academic ecosystem.

“Almost every aspect of IBM has an important presence here in India,” he said. “India is as important as every other center.”

Rao said IBM’s India engineering teams work across processor design, AI accelerators, quantum computing, and post-quantum cryptography (PQC), with additional teams working on Power processors, storage components, Linux, and some operating systems for Power processors. IBM’s consulting operations are also heavily concentrated in India. He described the approach as “talent arbitrage” rather than cost arbitrage.

“IBM believes there is a great amount of talent here, and we have to use that talent in the best possible way, wherever it makes sense,” he said.

IBM is separately establishing Anderon, a pure-play manufacturing foundry for quantum wafers, in Albany, New York. Rao called Anderon “the kitchen for qubits.” He said the foundry will use 300-mm wafers, the same standard size used in conventional CMOS manufacturing.

Rao said IBM’s roadmap over the next few years calls for scaling quantum processors from 200 and 300 qubits to 1,000 and eventually 4,000 qubits, building on the current Heron processor and an upcoming chip called Nighthawk.

“Achieving that scale requires the kind of robust manufacturing Anderon is meant to provide,” he said.

Post-quantum cryptography

At SEMICON India, IBM demonstrated a PQC process using an electronic know-your-customer (e-KYC) example. Rao explained that current public-key mechanisms such as Rivest-Shamir-Adleman (RSA) could be broken by a sufficiently powerful quantum computer. He said adversaries are already “harvesting” encrypted data today so they can decrypt it once such a computer becomes available.

IBM’s proposed approach is to introduce post-quantum algorithms, including ML-KEM for key exchange and ML-DSA for digital signatures, alongside existing algorithms during the transition.

For the RSA-based key exchange used in the e-KYC demo, Rao recommended starting with a hybrid approach.

“You retain the existing algorithms and layer ML-KEM with them,” he said.

The traditional algorithm can eventually be removed once organizations gain confidence in the new approach and complete the transition to PQC.

According to Rao, IBM systems can already execute PQC algorithms. He cited the IBM z17 system’s secure-boot capabilities, as well as the Crypto Express card, a hardware security module with FPGAs and accelerators to speed up PQC operations. Rao stopped short of providing performance figures for the card’s PQC acceleration, saying the work was still in the qualification phase.

PQC involves more complex mathematical operations, which can reduce performance when implemented conventionally.

“An organization capable of 10,000 authentications under standard algorithms might manage only one-tenth of that using PQC without acceleration,” Rao said.

Hardware acceleration is therefore being developed to recover some of that performance.

“Today, we provide software enablement, which people can buy,” he said. “It is available in the market. Hardware acceleration is part of the roadmap we are working on.”

IBM said it is also discussing proofs of concept with major public-sector institutions in India for hardware-accelerated PQC implementations. Rao pointed to work at the Indian Institute of Science (IISc) in Bangalore, where professor Utsav Banerjee has developed accelerator chips for PQC algorithms.

AI accelerators

ISDL is also involved in IBM’s Spyre AI accelerator, which has a 75-watt power envelope and is built around a die roughly 20 mm × 20 mm, containing 18 billion to 20 billion transistors, Rao said.

That works out, in his words, to “two transistors on this chip for every person on the planet.”

“A chip of that size can carry 20 billion to 40 billion transistors and 25 to 40 kilometers of wiring spread across 18 layers of metal,” he said. “It is not just about the physical arrangement. We have to ensure electrical robustness, mechanical sturdiness, and temperature reliability.”

The engineering also involves managing heat, cooling the chip, fitting it into the system, and maintaining power grid integrity.

“A lot of the Spyre accelerator work was done at ISDL,” Rao said. “The accelerator component was developed there, and much of the enablement work is also being done at ISDL.”

Open hardware

Rao also discussed IBM’s interest in open hardware, which he linked to the broader evolution of digital design.

“Just as we have open source in the software stack, there is open hardware,” he said.

As examples of the broader movement, he pointed to projects such as UC Berkeley’s Chipyard framework, Google’s OpenTitan root-of-trust chip, and open process design kits (PDKs). He also cited industry-standard components such as PCI Express that engineers can reuse rather than build from scratch.

Engineers should not need to develop every component themselves, Rao said.

“There is an entire world out there in open hardware,” he said. “There is Open PDK, which enables people to get access. It is almost like a democratization of digital design.”

He added that organizations still need to be aware that some information is restricted.

IBM’s own software approach combines open-source and proprietary components. Rao said the software stack around Power processors is essentially open source, with IBM among the top contributors to the Linux community.

“We have always believed in going open where it makes sense, which is higher up the stack, and being proprietary where you need an explicit component structure to ensure reliability, performance, and so on,” he said.

Rao pushed back on the idea that India’s role in global semiconductor development is limited to engineering execution. He pointed to patents filed by Indian inventors, papers with primarily Indian author lists, and IBM’s work on AI for scan-chain optimization using reinforcement learning, as well as design-technology co-optimization.

At SEMICON India, IBM’s model of the dilution refrigerator for the Quantum System Two, which is set to be installed in Amaravati, drew attention and prompted conversations. Its chandelier-like arrangement of gold wiring and cooling stages, dropping from 4 kelvin to the 10–20 millikelvin range where the quantum processing unit sits, showed the complexity of the setup.

In an earlier conversation with EE Times, Amith Singhee, CTO of IBM India and South Asia, described the arrangement. However, the scale of the model was difficult to appreciate until seen up close.

Alongside the refrigerator, IBM displayed information about the Anderon announcement, PQC demonstrations, and the Spyre accelerator card. Visitors moved between the exhibits, each representing a different part of the company’s work in advanced computing.

data.title: Calterah Turns UWB Digital Keys into In-Cabin Sensors

BARCELONA, Spain — As automotive safety regulators introduce stricter passenger-monitoring guidelines, carmakers face new engineering challenges. Vehicle interiors are filling up with different single-purpose sensors such as cameras, infrared detectors, and ultrasonic transducers. 

These devices help meet safety requirements, but adding more hardware raises manufacturing costs, complicates electrical systems, and creates space issues inside the car.

At last week’s InCabin Europe 2026 conference, Yaohui Liu, EMEA FAE and marketing manager at Calterah Semiconductor, shared a different approach using standardized wireless communication. Instead of adding more sensors to already crowded car interiors, Calterah proposed using existing ultra-wideband (UWB) digital key systems as a synchronized radar network. 

“We want to leverage the fact that more and more digital keys are occupying even basic models of cars, and we give them a new purpose, which is sensing,” Liu said. With the IEEE 802.15.4ab standard, synchronized UWB sensing is becoming a standard feature in cars worldwide.

Regulatory push for in-cabin sensing

Regulations and safety rating systems are the main drivers of carmakers’ adoption of advanced in-cabin sensing. The Euro NCAP 2026 standards will require higher safety levels and award top ratings to cars with child presence detection (CPD) systems that can sense small movements such as a baby’s breathing.

At the same time, the rise of consumer technology is speeding up UWB adoption. Billions of UWB-enabled devices, such as smartphones, smart tags, and digital key fobs, are now part of global supply chains.

According to Liu, Calterah Semiconductor, founded in Shanghai in 2014, has shipped over 30 million millimeter-wave radar chips to carmakers. Drawing on its automotive radar experience, the company claimed it now offers UWB chips that meet safety and monitoring needs without extra sensor housings.

Current safety rules require many types of internal monitoring, such as tracking driver alertness, checking if seats are occupied, verifying seatbelt use, and detecting unattended children, Liu said in his presentation. Using separate sensors for each task makes it hard for designers to fit everything inside the car. By turning existing UWB keyless entry anchors into a connected sensing network, Liu said carmakers can create a single system that covers all seating rows.

Overcoming the geometric traps of radar

Single-anchor radar systems inside a car cabin have ongoing physical limits. In his talk, Liu stressed that reliable interior monitoring is mainly a geometry issue, not just a matter of having more computing power or bigger AI models. “One thing I want to say is that it’s not really that a bigger AI model can solve everything, because we don’t want to burn our batteries just doing calculations,” Liu said. “What this UWB multi-static network gives you is really the geometry.”

He also argued that single-anchor radar nodes face internal signal leakage, where strong signals can block the receiver from detecting nearby objects. Adding more uncoordinated transceivers makes things worse, as their signals can interfere with each other and increase background noise.

“Synchronized multi-static UWB systems solve these geometry problems by placing sensors in different spots inside the car,” Liu said. “By putting transceivers in places like the rearview mirror, overhead console, and rear pillars, the system can see the cabin from several angles. If a baby in the third row is blocked from the front sensor, sensors in the rear pillars can still see them.”

Coordinated communication sensing network 

Unlike regular radar systems that send out uncoordinated signals, UWB works as a standardized wireless communication system. “The IEEE 802.15.4ab standard sets up a protocol that turns UWB radar into a network where devices can work together,” Liu said. “In this system, each UWB transceiver has a specific role, such as controller, transmitter, receiver, or requester.”

The standard uses a time-slotted media access control (MAC) layer organized into blocks, rounds, and slots. This careful scheduling allows digital key ranging and radar sensing to run simultaneously on the same hardware without signals interfering. When scheduled, one anchor sends out a signal while nearby anchors listen and measure the channel response.

The IEEE 802.15.4ab standard also adds frequency stitching across channels, such as Channels 9 and 10. Using several frequency bands increases bandwidth, improves spatial resolution, and reduces signal fading from metal surfaces inside the car.

After his talk, Liu sat down with EE Times for a short interview. He told us that coordinating the network is much more valuable than just adding more sensors. “It’s not like the more sensors the better, because there is a balance of feature scope, accuracy, and cost,” Liu said. “It is not necessarily that more is better, but that the technology can enable a network and coordinate—that gives you a big advantage.”

Eliminating sensor clutter and lowering cost

According to Liu, car manufacturers select sensing technologies based on strict factors such as cost, energy use, and design flexibility. Comparing UWB with cameras and ultrasonic sensors highlights key tradeoffs in these areas.

“While camera suites excel at two-dimensional image capture, computer vision algorithms struggle to extract accurate vertical height and depth information from flat images,” Liu told us. “Camera systems capture flat images well, but computer vision struggles to measure height and depth from them. Cameras also use a lot of power and do not work well in the dark or bright sunlight.”

Ultrasonic sensors, often used for parking, have limited accuracy and require holes in the car’s bumpers, which detract from the vehicle’s appearance. In rear parking assistance applications, this 3D spatial resolution lets the vehicle accurately assess obstacle height. As Liu illustrated, “You can measure exactly if the bumper is high enough that there is a curb you can drive over, or if you have to really stop before that.”

Liu pointed out the benefits of using fewer sensors: “Every sensor you add to the system, you have to qualify. The automotive qualification process is long, tedious, and costly. When you have one type of sensor qualified, you can use it for multi-purpose use—this is the ultimate dream come true.”

Silicon rollout and roadmap

Production-ready silicon chips now make synchronized UWB sensing possible for commercial use. Calterah’s Dubhe UWB platform uses a 2T4R transceiver setup for anchor nodes, which allows flexible antenna use for sending and receiving signals. For smartphones and key fobs, where distance measurement matters most, a simpler 1T4R design lowers costs while still working with the rest of the system.

In the same EE Times interview, Kamal Yanhansal, sales manager at Calterah, highlighted the role of advanced signal processing in meeting regulatory requirements. “With our 2T4R chip, we can enable 3D angle-of-arrival (AoA) where we see the benefit and we can enable the concept of virtual antennas,” he said. “We can achieve solid performance for advanced features like child presence detection and intrusion detection, showing the technology is capable of meeting standard requirements.”

The unified UWB anchor infrastructure supports a diverse stack of vehicle functions. Secure vehicle access and ranging operate under IEEE 802.15.4z-2020 and Car Connectivity Consortium (CCC) standards. Liu argued that the same transceivers perform IEEE 802.15.4ab bi-static and multi-static sensing for in-cabin child presence detection, occupant posture recognition, and exterior parking assistance. 

According to Liu, the transition to UWB sensing is part of a bigger trend toward software-defined vehicles. Since standardized transceivers are already being built into cars for digital keys, carmakers can add new safety, comfort, and monitoring features later through software updates.

“Today, the basic infrastructure is ready for the industry to deploy because the important thing is interoperability,” Liu concluded in the interview. “OEMs are not locked into one vendor. This is not a proprietary solution; it’s a standard-supported solution.” He added that the hardware foundation simplifies future vehicle updates: “You have the hardware already in the car supporting 802.15.4ab, and the rest is a software-defined vehicle where you add features on top of it—that is the journey for how OEMs and the industry adapt this technology.”

data.title: Xcena Cuts Data Movement to Address Memory Bottlenecks
data.description:
//php echo do_shortcode('[responsivevoice_button voice="US English Male" buttontext="Listen to Post"]') ?>

Processing data closer to memory is not a new idea, but South Korean startup Xcena believes it has a better way to do it by leveraging the Compute Express Link (CXL) protocol.

At Hot Chips 2026, the company detailed its MX1, a CXL Type 3 device that combines up to 2 TB of DDR5, SSD-backed InfiniteMemory capacity, and more than 1,000 custom RISC-V cores. Chief product officer Harry Kim said Xcena’s MX1 can deliver up to 4.7× the throughput and 18.7× the energy efficiency of a host CPU processing data over CXL on selected data analytics workloads.

In a briefing with EE Times, Kim said the memory bottleneck can’t be solved simply by adding more memory; existing memory resources must be used more efficiently. “If we can reduce the data movement, then it will be really helpful,” he said.

MX1 is particularly well suited to memory-intensive AI and database workloads where only a subset of stored data ultimately needs to be processed by CPUs or GPUs, Kim said.

For applications such as vector search, KV-cache operations, and database filtering, computation performed close to memory can reduce latency, power consumption, and bandwidth bottlenecks, he said. “For the database example, we can reduce data movement by filtering out the old data you don’t need to see from the CPU side.”

For AI, it means pulling just the relevant slice of a KV cache, Kim said.

Bringing together DDR5, SSDs, and RISC-V cores required solving significant software and memory management challenges because Xcena wanted to make the MX1 easy for customers to program, Kim said. “We want to keep the memory model as similar as what they want to do in the CPU side.”

He said one of the biggest technical hurdles was creating a unified virtual memory system capable of maintaining mappings between host memory, device memory, and SSD-backed capacity.

Xcena wanted MX1 to be, above all, a robust memory expander. Kim said it differentiates itself from competing CXL memory expansion products because it combines a full-featured memory controller with specialized near-memory processing capabilities. He said other computational CXL devices use general-purpose processors, while MX1 targets parallel data processing that uses all the internal bandwidth.

The device’s computational capabilities rely on a many-core RISC-V architecture, which Kim said was influenced by the maturity of the RISC-V ecosystem. The company modified an LLVM-based compiler to support custom instructions and offers a CUDA-like SDK, so developers can write in C, C++, or Rust.

Since managing thousands of processor cores remains challenging, Xcena developed a framework inspired by distributed database systems to simplify programming and workload management.

Xcena is sampling the MX1 prototype to memory vendors, CPU vendors, and hyperscalers, and the company plans mass production by the end of 2026, with initial customer revenue targeted for 2027.

Kim said a key dependency is broader industry adoption of CXL 3 running over PCIe 6.0, and while CXL adoption has been arguably slower than expected despite the rapid evolution of the protocol, he doesn’t think the technology itself is at fault, noting that all the CPU and GPU vendors, including Nvidia, have built CXL into their chips.

CXL is ready, Kim said, but its value still needs to be proven. Successful adoption requires a broader ecosystem, he said. “We need to prove CXL is good for everyone for AI infrastructure with CXL 3.”

In a briefing with EE Times, Jim Handy, principal analyst with Objective Analysis, said Xcena’s MX1 architecture is an interesting combination, similar to the approach taken by computational storage. “It’s an interesting product,” he said.

A recent Objective Analysis report, titled CXL Market Now Taking Shape, outlines how CXL is gaining adoption in the hyperscale computing community and how the technology now seems poised for significant growth.

Handy said one of the most appealing capabilities of CXL today is memory expansion, but repurposing older memory, such as DDR4, instead of buying DDR5 at current prices, has also become a common use case. He noted that Facebook parent company Meta is using CXL-based memory expansion across millions of servers, reusing DDR4 modules pulled from decommissioned machines rather than retiring them.

Handy said the memory pooling capability of CXL has yet to be widely used even though it’s a great idea. “There’s probably fire under the feet of the people who are developing pooling,” he said. “It improves the percent utilization that you get out of the memory chips you’ve already got, and if memory is really expensive, then you want to make sure that you’re not having any of it sitting around idle.”

//php echo do_shortcode('[responsivevoice_button voice="US English Male" buttontext="Listen to Post"]') ?>

In early September, Apple introduced the iPhone Duo, its first foldable iPhone, marking the company’s entry into a smartphone segment that other manufacturers have been developing for several years. Huawei, Samsung, and others already have had foldable devices on the market, including tri-fold models.

The Huawei Mate XT 2 Ultimate Design tri-fold smartphone has made headlines not only for its large screen and tri-fold mechanism, inherited from the previous generation, but also for the new processor powering it.

Alongside the Mate XT 2, Huawei has introduced its Kirin 9050 Pro processor, referred to as “Kirin 2026” in earlier technical material. The processor implements Huawei’s Tau (τ) Scaling Law, introduced by He Tingbo, president of Huawei’s semiconductor unit, at the 2026 IEEE International Symposium on Circuits and Systems.

With access to EUV lithography constrained, Huawei has developed a new chip design approach called LogicFolding. This technique stacks active silicon layers on top of each other, shortening signal paths and increasing transistor density.

From spatial geometry to temporal scaling

Because U.S. restrictions have blocked access to ASML’s EUV lithography equipment, Huawei has been seeking alternative ways to improve chip performance and density.

Conventional chip scaling, associated with Moore’s Law, has relied on shrinking transistor dimensions to increase transistor density. However, without advanced EUV lithography, thinner wires increase resistance and parasitic capacitance, which in turn slows the chip.

By focusing on how fast signals travel through the chip, LogicFolding addresses timing constraints. The technique improves digital, analog, and memory circuits across the stacked silicon layers by replacing long horizontal wires with short vertical connections. Huawei reported that this kind of vertical stacking reduces core routing lengths by 20% and shortens key timing paths by as much as 70%.

This new design also addresses heat issues. Because transferring data along horizontal wires accounts for more than 80% of a chip’s energy consumption, shorter signal paths reduce energy use. Huawei’s measurements, reported by TrendForce and EE Times China, indicate that power consumption fell by 66% for the neural processing unit, 58% for the graphics processing unit, and 41% for the CPU cores at comparable performance. To prevent the chip from overheating, Huawei has reduced operating voltages and clock speeds rather than increasing them.

Integrating 3D active layers presents formidable engineering and economic challenges. Mateo Valero, director of the Barcelona Supercomputing Center (BSC), told EE Times that as silicon scaling hits physical boundaries, transistor-level innovation alone is insufficient. “The transistor is important, but what matters now is how an entire system behaves,” Valero said, emphasizing that success depends on full-stack orchestration. “You have to co-design from the application all the way down to the transistor, software, system-on-chip architecture, and memory layout, or you run into bottlenecks elsewhere.”

Consumer deployment and the global performance gap

The Huawei Mate XT 2 Ultimate Design, which is equipped with the new processor, is a tri-fold smartphone priced from 19,999 yuan (~$2,980) to 24,999 yuan (~$3,725). Sales began Sept. 12 and are currently limited to the Chinese market.

The chip features a nine-core CPU, with the primary core operating at 3.1 GHz, a Maleoon 920 GPU that supports hardware ray tracing up to 50 million rays per second, and a Da Vinci neural processing unit capable of running a 30-billion-parameter Mixture-of-Experts AI model directly on the device.

Manufacturing realities, foundry friction, and economic cost

Even with its new design, LogicFolding makes the manufacturing process much more complicated. SMIC has produced 7-nm-class chips without EUV lithography, and the Kirin 9050 Pro is believed to use a similar process, although Huawei has not disclosed the chip’s foundry or process node. The chip package incorporates two active layers and a 1.5-µm hybrid-bonding pitch, with approximately 50 million vertical connections, 10% to 15% of which carry active signals.

Huawei said its Kirin 2027 test silicon has already lowered the hybrid-bonding pitch to 1 µm, with more than 100 million vertical interconnects. Over the next three years, the company said it aims to achieve a pitch of 720 nm. By 2031, it targets a transistor density equivalent to a 1.4-nm process.

However, manufacturing yields suffer when active logic layers are connected directly. The process requires extremely accurate wafer thinning and smoothing to prevent small gaps, and misalignment of the copper pads can cause wiring problems and warping.

Addressing these hurdles, Valero observed that “unless memory arrangement, compilers, and hardware scheduling are seamlessly orchestrated, isolated architectural tricks cannot overcome physical manufacturing constraints.”

In the first half of 2026, Huawei’s R&D expenditure increased 25.2% year on year to 121.38 billion yuan (~$18.13 billion), equivalent to 25.9% of revenue. Meanwhile, net profit fell 36% to 23.81 billion yuan. U.S. export restrictions have forced Huawei to invest heavily in self-reliant AI and chip capabilities. Higher R&D costs, alongside rising memory chip prices, are continuing to weigh on the company’s overall profitability and consumer business.

LinxISA versus Arm and RISC-V

To protect its hardware from geopolitical risks, Huawei has moved away from standard instruction set architectures. Although the company holds a permanent license for the older Armv8 architecture, U.S. export laws still pose regulatory risks for using the newer Armv9 architecture.

To address these problems, Huawei is reportedly developing LinxISA, a block-structured instruction set architecture. Unlike Arm or RISC-V, which execute instructions one at a time, LinxISA executes instructions in blocks. Its use in the Kirin 9050 Pro has not been publicly confirmed.

Valero told EE Times that hardware decisions cannot be viewed in isolation, noting that optimizing individual hardware parts without full orchestration creates performance bottlenecks across the stack.

Software autonomy and enterprise compute ambitions

Huawei has released HarmonyOS 7, which doesn’t use any open-source Android code and relies on its own microkernel and EROFS file system.

Huawei said it intends to apply LogicFolding not just to its smartphones but also to its enterprise data centers and, by 2030, plans to launch the Ascend 990 AI chip to compete with Nvidia and Alibaba. On these end-to-end integration efforts, Valero remarked to EE Times that when architectural teams optimize “from top to bottom,” they can build systems “that claim to compete against Nvidia.”

Huawei is seeking to expand the domestic semiconductor equipment supply chain, alongside Chinese suppliers such as AMEC and NAURA, which are developing equipment for processes including etching, deposition, and advanced packaging. By bringing these different stages together, Huawei hopes to create a self-sufficient technology ecosystem for the development of advanced chips.

data.title: Delos Data Targets Heterogeneous AI With Data Interface
